steps.caption: Every blood cell comes from the **hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)** in the bone marrow. It can renew itself and also commit to making new cells.
The HSC first splits into two branches. The **common myeloid progenitor (CMP, CFU-GEMM)** makes everything except lymphocytes; the **common lymphoid progenitor (CLP)** makes lymphocytes.
From the CMP, megakaryocytes shed **platelets** under **thrombopoietin (TPO)**, made mainly by the liver. Erythroid cells become red cells under **erythropoietin (EPO)**, made by the kidney.
The **granulocyte–monocyte progenitor (GMP, CFU-GM)**, driven by GM-CSF, makes neutrophils (G-CSF), eosinophils (IL-5), basophils, and monocytes (M-CSF), which become macrophages in tissue.
The **common lymphoid progenitor**, supported by IL-7, makes B cells, T cells (which mature in the thymus) and NK cells.

**Takeaway:** myeloid = red cells, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes; lymphoid = B, T and NK cells. Match each cell line to its growth factor: EPO for red cells, TPO for platelets, G-CSF for neutrophils.

visuals.alt: A family tree. The hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) branches into the common myeloid progenitor (CMP, CFU-GEMM) and the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP). The CMP gives megakaryocytes and platelets (growth factor TPO), erythroid cells and red cells (EPO), and the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor (GMP, CFU-GM; GM-CSF), which gives neutrophils (G-CSF), eosinophils (IL-5), basophils, and monocytes that become macrophages (M-CSF). The CLP (IL-7) gives B cells, T cells (matured in the thymus) and NK cells.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Facts per Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications 7e, hematopoiesis chapter.

steps.caption: This is the **laboratory (test-tube) model** of coagulation. The **extrinsic pathway** starts when tissue factor (TF), exposed by injured tissue, binds factor VIIa.
The **intrinsic pathway** starts with contact activation of factor XII (with prekallikrein and HMWK). XIa activates IX, and IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates X.

Both pathways meet at **factor X**, the start of the **common pathway**. Xa with cofactor Va turns prothrombin (II) into thrombin, thrombin turns fibrinogen (I) into fibrin, and XIIIa cross-links the fibrin.
The **PT/INR** tests the extrinsic and common pathways: factors VII, X, V, II and I. It is the test used to monitor warfarin.
The **APTT** tests the intrinsic and common pathways: XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and I. It is prolonged in hemophilia A (VIII) and B (IX) and by unfractionated heparin.

Factors **II, VII, IX and X** need vitamin K for γ-carboxylation in the liver, without which they cannot bind calcium (proteins C and S also need it). Warfarin or vitamin K deficiency lowers all four; VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT prolongs first.

**Takeaway:** PT = extrinsic + common, APTT = intrinsic + common, and neither detects factor XIII deficiency. In the body, clotting follows the **cell-based model**: TF–VIIa starts it, and XI, IX and VIII amplify it on platelets; XII is not needed, so XII deficiency prolongs the APTT without bleeding.

visuals.alt: The laboratory model of the coagulation cascade. Intrinsic pathway: XII to XIIa, XI to XIa, IX to IXa with VIIIa. Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor with VIIa. Both activate X; the common pathway continues Xa with Va, prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa), fibrinogen (I) to fibrin, and XIIIa cross-linking fibrin. A bracket marks the APTT over the intrinsic and common pathways and another marks the PT/INR over the extrinsic and common pathways, both stopping before XIII. Factors II, VII, IX and X carry a K badge for vitamin K dependence.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Facts per Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications 7e, normal hemostasis and coagulation testing chapters.

visuals.subject: HE
visuals.title: Neutrophil maturation: blast to segmented cell

steps.caption: The **myeloblast** is the first recognisable cell in the line: large, with fine chromatin, **visible nucleoli** and blue cytoplasm, with no granules or only a few primary granules.
The **promyelocyte** makes the **primary (azurophilic) granules**, which hold myeloperoxidase. Nucleoli can still be seen.
**Secondary (specific) granules** first appear in the **myelocyte**, and nucleoli are no longer seen. The myelocyte is the **last stage that can divide**.

After that, cells only mature. The **metamyelocyte** nucleus indents into a kidney shape (indent less than half the width of the nucleus); in the **band** the indent passes the halfway point and the nucleus narrows into a curved band of even width.
The **segmented neutrophil** has 2–5 lobes joined by thin chromatin filaments. Bands and segmented cells are the forms normally seen in blood.
**Takeaway:** nucleoli end after the promyelocyte, primary granules start in the promyelocyte, secondary granules in the myelocyte, and cell division stops after the myelocyte.

visuals.alt: Six schematic cells from top to bottom. 1 Myeloblast: large round nucleus with two nucleoli, no granules or only a few. 2 Promyelocyte: larger cell with many dark primary (azurophilic) granules and a nucleolus. 3 Myelocyte: round eccentric nucleus without nucleoli and many fine secondary (specific) granules. A dashed line below the myelocyte separates the stages that can divide from those that only mature. 4 Metamyelocyte: kidney-shaped nucleus, indented less than half its width. 5 Band: curved band-shaped nucleus of even width. 6 Segmented neutrophil: 2 to 5 lobes joined by thin filaments.
visuals.source: Original schematic drawings (not to scale). Facts per Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications 7e, leukocyte development chapter.

visuals.subject: HE
visuals.title: RBC indices and the RBC histogram

steps.caption: The **RBC indices** are calculated from the RBC count, hemoglobin and hematocrit. Example: Hct 32% and RBC 4.20 × 10¹²/L give MCV = 32 × 10 ÷ 4.20 = **76.2 fL**.
The analyzer also draws an **RBC histogram**: number of cells against cell volume. A normal curve is a single bell centred near 90 fL, and its centre matches the **MCV**.
A curve **shifted left** means small cells: **microcytic**, MCV below 80 fL, as in iron deficiency or thalassemia.
A curve **shifted right** means large cells: **macrocytic**, MCV above 100 fL, as in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
The **RDW** (red cell distribution width) is the width of the curve: how much cell sizes vary. A wide curve and a high RDW mean **anisocytosis**, as in iron deficiency.
**Takeaway:** the MCV tells where the curve sits and the RDW tells how wide it is. An MCHC above about 36 g/dL suggests spherocytes or an artefact such as cold agglutinins or lipemia.

visuals.alt: Top: RBC index formulas. MCV = Hct x 10 / RBC, in fL, about 80-100. MCH = Hb x 10 / RBC, in pg. MCHC = Hb x 100 / Hct, in g/dL, about 32-36. Units: RBC x10^12/L, Hb g/dL, Hct %. Bottom: an RBC histogram of number of cells against cell volume (fL). The normal curve is a bell centred near 90 fL, at the MCV. A microcytic curve is shifted left and a macrocytic curve is shifted right. The RDW is the width of the curve; a wider, flatter curve means a high RDW (anisocytosis).
visuals.source: Original diagram. Formulas and reference intervals per Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications 7e (examination of blood and automated cell counting chapters). Reference intervals vary by laboratory.

To stop additive carryover.</text><text x="24" y="524" class="v-text v-small">EDTA carried into a serum or heparin tube:</text><text x="24" y="542" class="v-text v-small">K⁺ falsely high, Ca²⁺ falsely low.</text></g>

steps.caption: **Blood culture** bottles are filled first, so they are collected under the most sterile conditions.

Next the **light blue (sodium citrate)** tube for coagulation tests, before any tube whose clot activator or other additive could affect it. Fill it to the line to keep the **9:1** blood-to-citrate ratio.
Then **serum tubes**: red (plain or with clot activator) and gold (clot activator plus separator gel).
Then **green (heparin)** tubes, lithium or sodium heparin, for plasma chemistry.
Then **lavender (K₂EDTA)** for the CBC. It comes late because EDTA carried into a chemistry tube **raises K⁺** (it is a potassium salt) and **lowers Ca²⁺** (it binds calcium).
Last, **gray (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate)** for glucose and lactate. Fluoride stops glycolysis; oxalate, like EDTA, would add potassium and remove calcium, so it goes last.
**Takeaway:** blood culture → light blue → red/gold → green → lavender → gray. The order exists to prevent **additive carryover** between tubes.

visuals.alt: Six rows in CLSI order of draw. 1 Blood culture bottles, sterile, first. 2 Light blue cap, sodium citrate, filled to the line (9:1), for PT and APTT. 3 Red or gold cap, serum tubes with or without clot activator and gel. 4 Green cap, lithium or sodium heparin, plasma chemistry. 5 Lavender cap, K2EDTA, CBC and smear. 6 Gray cap, sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, glucose and lactate. A note explains the order prevents additive carryover: EDTA carried into a serum or heparin tube falsely raises potassium and falsely lowers calcium.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Order per CLSI GP41 (Collection of Diagnostic Venous Blood Specimens); see also Rodak's Hematology 7e, blood specimen collection chapter. Cap colours vary slightly by manufacturer.

steps.caption: **Fibrinolysis** dissolves clots once they have done their job. Plasminogen bound to fibrin is turned into **plasmin** by tissue plasminogen activator (**tPA**, from endothelial cells) or urokinase (**uPA**).
Plasmin cuts fibrinogen and non-cross-linked fibrin into **fibrin(ogen) degradation products (FDPs)**: fragments X, Y, D and E.
Fibrin that factor XIIIa has cross-linked breaks down into **D-dimer**: two D domains still joined by the cross-link. So D-dimer shows that a real clot formed and was then lysed.
Two inhibitors act as brakes: **PAI-1** blocks tPA and uPA, and **α2-antiplasmin** inactivates free plasmin.

A **raised D-dimer** means a clot formed and is being broken down, as in DVT, pulmonary embolism or DIC; it also rises after surgery and in pregnancy. A **normal D-dimer** helps rule out venous thromboembolism.
**Takeaway:** tPA and uPA make plasmin; plasmin makes FDPs from fibrin(ogen) but D-dimer only from cross-linked fibrin; PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin hold it back.

visuals.alt: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tPA and uPA; PAI-1 inhibits the activators and alpha-2-antiplasmin inhibits plasmin. Plasmin breaks fibrinogen and non-cross-linked fibrin into FDPs (fragments X, Y, D and E) and breaks fibrin cross-linked by factor XIIIa into D-dimer. A note says a raised D-dimer means a clot formed and is being broken down (DVT, pulmonary embolism, DIC), and a normal D-dimer helps rule out venous thromboembolism.
